claims.text: Conventionally synthesized multi-element near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles generally have a largely random, minimally ordered chemical structure.
Extended elevated-temperature annealing promotes local chemical order in these nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching can lock in the local chemical order produced during annealing.
High-resolution TEM and synchrotron X-ray diffraction can quantify the degree of local chemical order in the nanoparticles.
Greater local chemical order raises migration-energy barriers for defect formation.
Greater local chemical order raises migration-energy barriers for atomic diffusion.
Reduced defect mobility suppresses nanoparticle coarsening.
Reduced defect mobility suppresses phase separation.
Multi-element alloy nanoparticles can retain uniform dispersion, size stability, and a homogeneous single-phase alloy structure during heating to 873 K.
Annealed-and-quenched nanoparticles with enhanced local chemical order will coarsen more slowly than untreated nanoparticles.
Annealed-and-quenched nanoparticles with enhanced local chemical order will retain phase integrity better than untreated nanoparticles.
Annealed-and-quenched nanoparticles with enhanced local chemical order will retain chemical homogeneity better than untreated nanoparticles.
The proposed local-order stabilization effect applies throughout catalytic service temperatures of 773–1173 K.
The proposed local-order stabilization effect applies throughout thermoelectric service temperatures of 473–1923 K.
Enhanced local chemical order can stabilize these nanoparticles even when their noble-metal content is low.
The expected effect may depend on elemental composition and on whether service conditions fall within the stated temperature windows.
Impurities and support interactions may influence the magnitude of the stability improvement.
The cited prior evidence specifically supports a stabilizing role for local chemical order.
